utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we begin in the usual manner by recording today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a couple of matters before the witness comes in. First is, I don't know whether Your Honours have had a chance to look at the diagram of the makeup of the CSB and the SJB in Banja Luka. It was based on the -- effectively the first 54 pages of the interview that was conducted with the witness -- with Mr. Tutus in Banja Luka in 2004, and rather than go through it all, we thought the simplest thing to do would be to reduce it to one of these charts again. Because Mr. Tutus couldn't check it until yesterday, and he made some alterations to the original chart, we couldn't actually disclose it until this morning. I understand that -- my learned friend -- Mr. Zecevic does not object. Mr. Krgovic, I think, wants to be able to check with it Zupljanin first but is prepared, I think, to let it go in subject to any matters that may arise, so that's the first thing. Your Honours, the second matter is this. I don't know whether Your Honours had a chance to read the proofing note. You'll there's a reference there to the ill health which the witness suffers from. Now, I know he went to see the doctor this morning. I did ask VWS if they could let me know there were any problems. I heard nothing, so I'm assuming, optimistically, that there are none. I asked him what the situation was about reading documents, and he says he thinks he's all right. He'd prefer, as it were, read to him, and to follow than to try and read himself, and I think it's actually going to be easier on the screen because we can highlight and enlarge the various bits rather and being given a bundle of documents. But I'm simply alerting Your Honours to it. I think the more possibility -- the more -- the greater problem may be the high blood pressure. I -- I hope Your Honours will forgive me, I told him that if he felt unwell at all, he should immediately let Your Honours know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, our current advice is that the witness having been seen by the medical staff this morning is well at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I do no more than alert you to a potential problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had given notice that I wished to raise one matter before the Trial Chamber before the witness is ushered in. I had already discussed it with Ms. Korner and it does relate precisely to the health of the witness. The point is, the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka did the forensic expertise for all the public security stations covered by the CSB. The CSB Banja Luka, or, rather, the archive of that centre, is the only CSB archive which has been mostly preserved and since it was seized by IFOR units in 1998, it has been in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor. From the viewpoint of the Prosecution, according to the indictment and the pre-trial brief, investigations against perpetrators in areas where the victims were Muslim or Croat, or non-Serbs, were not properly done, and, in that sense, the forensic material found in the archive of the CSB Banja Luka is very relevant to this case. In the course of my interview that I had with this witness last Saturday, I showed to him some of these documents and he identified some of them and discussed them. However, since this concerns a relatively large amount of material, I thought, precisely in view of the health of this witness, I should suggest the application of the same procedure as with Ms. Hanson. The witness would identify a few of the documents and the rest, according to the list, would be made available to the Trial Chamber subsequently with an application that they be admitted. Because these documents are more or less identical; reports on the taking of finger-prints, the paraffin glove test, et cetera. I wanted to spare the witness the effort of looking through the entirety of the documents and to save time, of course, and that is why I thought I would suggest this course of action. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I -- I don't know that there would be any objection to this course, but the Chamber does have a question that perhaps you -- on which you could perhaps assist. And that is the method by which the -- we can be satisfied that the specimen documents which the witness proves while in court corresponds to the -- is -- is an accurate reflection of the bulk of the documents, if you follow my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will try to explain. Your Honours, the witness cannot confirm each and every document, obviously. But, first of all, it is not within the SJB Banja Luka but within -- within the CSB Banja Luka, this criminal technical department or forensic department. But being in the same building where the CSB was situated at the time, he knows the procedure and, in fact, he, as the -- as the chief of SJB, also used the -- used the -- CSB technical department in some cases where they were investigating some serious crimes. Now, I'm not -- I am -- I'm really not sure to give you any -- any -- any additional explanation, except as far as I can see, all these documents have -- are sort of a form on the first side, and then they contain some -- some data which are -- which are connected to a -- to a certain crime. If -- if -- if it pleases Your Honours, we can probably MFI these documents, but then, again, we would be required to bring another witness to -- to confirm the contents of these documents, probably from the forensic department. I was -- I was of opinion that -- that my learned colleague from the -- from the Prosecution side does not object to this, and therefore I -- I tried to shortcut the -- the admission of these documents, because I think we -- they are relevant and we will rely on that. Now, if -- of course, it is in the hands of Your Honour and I will accept whatever the ruling will be. I hope I was of any assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Obviously we don't get to see the documents until they're released by the Defence once the witness starts. And my understanding is that -- that the witness can talk about the procedure, may know about some of the files but not the others. If it assists Mr. Zecevic, we are, of course, calling a number of different prosecutors and can probably deal with the documents if they're all part of a criminal file. However, having said that, provided that we're assured that these are all documents that come from the CSB archives, then I don't see that we'll be raising any objection to this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the -- the issue that is being put before the Chamber in respect of your proposal is that the Chamber has to be fully aware of the contents of every piece of document that we admit into evidence. So we will go along -- or we could go along with your proposal, provided that we can rely on your assessments that these documents are very similar in nature and kind. Because if -- if -- if you cannot -- if are you telling us that -- that the documents cover a broad range of issues, then we would have a difficulty to import them en bloc, if you see what I mean. So the only -- the fundamental condition that we have to put in order to accept your proposal is that once you have shown us two or three of the documents, we can be sure that the remaining bulk of the documents are really the same in kind and nature. If not, then we will have to develop another procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly, Your Honours, what I intended to do. They are mainly two or maybe three groups of documents. One is the taking of the -- so-called paraffin glove, which would -- which is a procedure to establish, if the certain person has used the fire -- fire-arm. That is one -- that is one group of documents. The other group of documents is -- are the documents where -- where they are -- where they are actually taking the finger-prints from the victims, trying to establish the identity of the victims. That's the second. And the third group of documents refers to the cases of searches for explosive materials and some arson is -- which were happening in the territory. So that is -- as far as I -- as I -- as I have been able to -- to identify, those are the three groups of the documents. And they're basically, of course, containing different -- different data in them because they refer to a specific case, but in their general nature, they are completely identical documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the usher -- if the usher would kindly escort the witness in [Microphone not activated]. Ms. Korner, there are no protective measures for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, there aren't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. You may be seated. Would you tell us your name, your profession, and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vladimir Tutus, born on the 15th of October, 1953, in Sanski Most. I have a degree in law, specialisation in security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you say you have a degree in law. Is -- did you work as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I -- I have a degree in law, and I have worked as a lawyer specialising in security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you previously testified before this Tribunal or in the region of the former Yugoslavia, in any of the countries that comprise that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have not testified before this Tribunal before. I did testify, however, in a number of cases before the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- or, rather, one case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's in my proofing notes, but nothing to do with war crimes at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. The -- you have been called as a witness by the Prosecution before this Tribunal, and the procedure is that the side calling you - in this case, the Prosecution - would begin by asking you questions, and the -- when they would have concluded, then the -- it is open to counsel for each of the accused to ask questions of you, if they wish. Following that, the Prosecution has the opportunity to re-examine you on matters that would have arisen out of cross-examination. And when the lawyers are finished, then the Chamber itself may have questions of you. You are scheduled to testify -- it is anticipated that your testimony will occupy a number of days, and the -- as may have been pointed out to you, the -- we would have begun today's session in the afternoon, but for the remainder of the week, the sessions are in the morning session -- in the morning beginning at 9.00, except Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Wednesday when we aren't sitting, and then Friday again we are in the afternoon. The sessions are not continuous, although the -- the length of time for each day is four hours it is not a continuous period. There are breaks after not more than 90 minutes for technical and other reasons which allows you to time to refresh yourself. And the -- with that, I would invite counsel for the Prosecution, Ms. Korner, to begin her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tutus, I want to begin with how you come to be at this court. I think it's right that you were interviewed in 2001 in Banja Luka by the Office of the Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were interviewed as a witness on that occasion. In 2004, again, were you interviewed at some length by the Office of the Prosecutor, but this time with the status of a suspect?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours can I just make it clear I think so that you don't wonder why there was a change. It's not that there was further evidence found between 2001 and 2004. It was simply that in 2001 it was decided that the witnesses -- the persons who were interviewed who had been a party to the events could be interviewed as witnesses. By 2004 it was decided that technically, if nothing else, they came within the provisions of the -- the rule which qualifies them to be suspects. So it's not that there was a sudden change. I think in fairness to the witness that should be said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's also right, Mr. Tutus, that you are here today because a summons was issued bringing you to the court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, I received a summons from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You were able to see and speak to Defence counsel from both teams, that is Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin, on the Saturday, when you -- that is, last Saturday, the 13th of March; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were -- you spent yesterday, and I'm sorry it took so long, going through the various documents that -- some of which, not all, you will be happy to hear, I'm going to ask you to look at. Now, can I start, first of all, with your career very shortly. You told the Trial Chamber you had a law degree. I think it's right that you began your career as a police officer in Banja Luka in 1973; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were then sent by the police for further schooling and training in Zagreb, and it's, I think it's right, that you then went to university, completing that in 1980. And is that when you got your law degree?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I finished the College for Internal Affairs in Zagreb and I became, by profession, a lawyer, so -- specialised in crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. However, did you then return to the police force and -- I'm going to skip a bit of your career, because, in 1990, after the multi-party elections, did you become the chief of the SJB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think it's right that you -- you know Mico Stanisic. And can you tell the Court how long you have known him?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So was that when you were, in fact, still at school?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Stojan Zupljanin, when did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: As far as can I remember, it was around 1975, when he started working in the SUP in Banja Luka. I was already working at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, again, by 1990, you'd known him for some 15 years or so?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were at school with Mico Stanisic, but did you ever work with him professionally as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I worked in Banja Luka, and Mico worked in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. He answered the question. All right. Can I just ask you next about some general questions about Banja Luka. First of all, I'd like you to have a look at a map of Banja Luka, which shows the ethnic national distribution which is number 10236.01. I'm afraid, Mr. Tutus, it sometimes takes a little bit of time to load this onto the screen. Thank you. First of all, that shows that the census in 1991 showed that there were 29.000 Croats, 106 -- nearly 107.000 Serbs, 28.000 -- 28.500 Muslims, and just over 23.500 people who described themselves as Yugoslavs in Banja Luka. Does that accord with your recollection? I mean, it's actually a census figure, so ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I wasn't concerned with statistics that related to the population. But if this is official data from the census, then I have no reason to doubt the correctness of the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, really, the effect is that Banja Luka was, as far as the nationality went -- a sizeable majority was Serbs. Would you agree with that, from your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you -- if we pull the map up a bit so we can see the -- the distribution, as it were, again, that shows the various villages around the town of Banja Luka and the majority makeup of each village. Again, does that accord with your knowledge of the area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, I can't see these villages very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: It's a little blurred. I can see Bastasi here in green. That village was inhabited by Muslims, by Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That's fine. I don't -- I don't think we need trouble you -- I don't want you to strain your eyes, Mr. Tutus. As far as the town of Banja --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as the town of Banja Luka is concerned, were there certain areas within the town that were more heavily populated by Bosniaks or Croats?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: On the whole, the population of Banja Luka was mixed. There were certain urban area, however, where the majority were citizens of other nationalities, for example, in Vrbanja. In Vrbanja there was a concentration of Muslims that. Would be one example.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What about the Mejdan area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's in that area, in the Mejdan and Vrbanja area. It goes on towards Celinac, then in direction of Seher in Desa Novoselija, that area was also inhabited by the Muslims. They were concentrated there. That was in Desa Novoselija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that it be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1075, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, can I just ask you to look, please, at a photograph of the CSB itself, which is -- which is ... yeah, 3419.28. And this is a recent photograph. But can you tell us, we know that the CSB and the SJB in Banja Luka shared the same premises in Banja Luka. Which floor was the SJB based on, or was it more than one floor?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: It was on the first floor. That's where my office was in the SJB. And we had certain offices on the fourth floor as well. And also on the ground floor, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll have a look at your -- or the diagrammatical representation of what you explained about the various personnel in the SJB and the CSB. But did you share a communications centre?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, we had a joint one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I -- has that been exhibited? It's not been exhibited yet. Could I ask that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1076, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tutus, you actually spent a very long time with Mr. Sebire helpfully explaining who was who in the SJB and the CSB, and you've had a chance to look at a diagram that was produced by us. You made some corrections, and I'd like you now to have a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 10138.12. Now, we're going to have to enlarge this quite a lot for anybody to see anything. All right. Can we start, please, if we -- can we move the CSB part over, which is the right-hand side, so we can get a look at the left-hand side and enlarge it? All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Tutus, now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a lot better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we see yourself there as the chief. And then do we see --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Divided up the various sections which were contained within the SJB, that is, the crime section of which Mr. Zoran Josic, I hope, was the chief, the traffic safety section. Is that right, it was taken in May or June of 1992, it was simply put into the CSB?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Djuro Bulic, who was the commander of the traffic safety section, in fact, was he moved to the CSB and he became the deputy to Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: He moved a little earlier. Prior to the traffic safety station being moved, he moved a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then under that, do we see --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we just move the thing slightly to the left, not under, sorry, across, I mean, can we move across slightly because there is one thing that doesn't show up. Can we move the document to the left. Yes, thank you. Were these what I call the substations which came within your jurisdiction, that is, the Centar, Budzak, and Mejdan?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there we see the various people who were the commanders of that station. Now we see under Vinko - is it? - Riling?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That -- the words "did not sign." Does that refer to the solemn declaration that was -- that the -- that the police in Banja Luka had to sign after April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: It concerns the solemn declaration that all employees of the service had to sign. Not just employees of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You say all employees. All employees in the MUP or all employees in whatever kind of enterprise they were engaged?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: All employees in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what nationality was Mr. Riling?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then he was replaced by Mr. Miskic. In Mejdan --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just move it a bit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see Mirsad Beharic was the commander. Same thing, he didn't sign, so -- and was he -- I think we can all tell from that, he was a Bosniak, or a Muslim, as it was in those day?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To be replaced by Mr. -- that one's a difficult. Can you say that name, the one below, who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Petar Tanazovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, finally, Radomir Rodic, replaced him?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to -- can we move it to the right again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was also a legal and administration section, and she was moved -- I'm not sure what 09 is supposed to stand for. Moved to 09. Oh, I see, is that the line? Yeah. It's the personnel -- yeah. Did she move to the CSB? Yes, I think we can see that she did.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, she was moved to the CSB a little later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to -- I think that's all we need to do on the SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just have a quick look at the CSB diagram. So if we move the document back to getting -- so we get to the CSB. Right up, yeah, right across, thanks, and then up again. No, sorry, I want to go down to the bit of the diagram that shows the CSB, which is to the right. Yes, no, I think ... other way. If you move the document to the left, the whole big document and let's get on to the CSB. Yeah, thank you. And a bit more. Can we start at the top of the document. We seem to have lost -- no, move the document to the left, please. Great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Banja Luka CSB, Stojan Zupljanin, and then his secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we -- sorry, can we go down the document again to where we were, to Mr. Jahic. A bit -- can we move the document to the right, please. No, to the right. Great. Stop. Thank you. And a bit further up. Can we -- could I have the top bit of that part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Originally, it says right up until April of 1992, again with the solemn declaration, the deputy chief of the centre was Mr. Jahic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That's not correct. Bajazid Jahic was the chief of the sector of public security. There was no deputy position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Was -- so the chief of the -- the -- the sorry. So the chief of the -- I'm sorry, let me just have a look. They haven't caught what you said on LiveNote either. What did you say he was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I said that there was not a position of deputy chief of the CSB. Bajazid Jahic was the chief of the sector for public security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sorry. Did you correct that when you saw that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that it's incorrect. You said deputy. I don't see the deputies written here. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So he's the chief of the ... the chief of sector for public security. In reality, did that mean that -- that whoever was chief of the security of public security acted as a deputy to Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: You cannot look at it that way. He headed the public security sector which included other services as well. There was no deputy chief. He was responsible for the part of the service that he headed. That's all it meant. When the chief of the centre would be absent, or was about to go away somewhere, then he would, himself, designate a stand-in. There were two sectors within that service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when he was designating that stand-in, was it normally the chief of that sector for public security. Mr. Tutus, did you hear the question? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard the question. But I can't give you a precise answer. I don't know to whom the chief of the centre assigned his powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In any event, is it right that Mr. Bulic did replace Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then you've said that we've set out all the -- the various sections which came under the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we just move the document so that we can look at the Department for Analysis and Information for a moment, which means moving the document to the left. Yes, just stop there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The lady we see there, Fatima Ejupovic-Hrnic. What nationality was she?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I think she was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. How long did she -- if you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go down the document a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see she was replaced eventually by somebody called Cubrilovic. How long did she stay? Do you remember, when did she leave the CSB?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: They worked in analysis. I don't think the analysis section had a chief, or at least I don't know who the chief was. But they -- the two of them, worked together in analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So do you know when Ms. Ejupovic-Hrnic left the CSB, stopped working for them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think it was sometime in 1992. Perhaps mid-1992. She didn't leave immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You were asked about this in your interview. Would it be right to say that effectively by the end of 1992 both the CSB and the SJB in Banja Luka contained only employees who were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: You couldn't say that that way. Everyone had to state their nationality individually. Plus, there were people from mixed marriages and you could not look at it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't want to ask anything more about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask they be admitted, E and O, for any -- we may remove -- we may later replace by removing the words "deputy chief," but in any event, could it be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I just wish to confirm that there is no objection from the Defence? I think there's the indication we'd had earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. The Stanisic Defence does not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1077, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tutus, now I want to move to some of the events of 1992. In particular, I want to start with the meeting of February the 11th. I think we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I may need just a moment. Your Honour, I'm sorry, something went wrong with the dates when they came out. They came out American style, so they're not in chronological order. So there may be a delay while I just work out where I want to start.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It will come up in a moment, Mr. ... Now, you were shown this document when you were interviewed in 2004. You -- you did attend this meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Where was this meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, in, we've heard, the Hotel Bosna.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, I probably did, if it's written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, your name on -- appears --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: All right. I've just seen it when I put on my glasses. Yes, I agree I was there. I cannot identify the place. I cannot remember I was on that location, but I am not going to go as far as to dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- the assembled company who were there were all reasonably high-up members of -- Serbian members of the MUP, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go through the entire list. But I believe it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You -- you also knew, I think, didn't you, Momcilo Mandic, again, since school?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we've dealt with Mico Stanisic. Did you know Cedo Kljajic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I knew him. Kljajic is the name, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Slavko Draskovic. I mean, rather than taking you through the whole lot now, it must -- how usual was it to have a meeting like this held not in the CSB but in the Hotel Bosna?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Depends on the organiser. The usual custom is to hold it on the premises of organs of internal affairs. But it could be held elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember how you got an invitation to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could we go, please, in the document to the third page in English and to the fourth page, I -- yeah. To the fourth page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The minute-taker, Mr. Vilasovic [phoen], recorded you as speaking at this meeting starting by saying: "The people of Bosanska Krajina have lost trust in the Serbian leadership of the MUP as well as the entire BH MUP." Now by "the people of Bosanska Krajina," did you mean the population as a whole or members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need to bring the B/C/S up a bit for the witness. The B/C/S, not the English.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I did not revise this text before the transcript was made, but if I said the people of Bosanska Krajina, I certainly couldn't have been speaking on behalf of the entire people. I was speaking on behalf of the service I was heading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And by "the Serbian leadership of the MUP," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, I meant all of them who were working there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say "all of them," all of them where?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I meant all of them who were working in the top leadership of the MUP of Republika Srpska [as interpreted], because I felt that from the very first day when I went out to talk to them, and later the dispatches that came down were inappropriate, and you could not feel the representation of Serbian staff in the MUP in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And your complaint largely seems to be that the equipment that was being provided was inadequate; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner. Just for the clarity -- for the clarity of the transcript, it's recorded that the witness said "leadership of the MUP of Republika Srpska." However, I mean, you could clarify that. I believe he meant something else. But -- but said MUP of Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think you were referring there to the MUP of -- of BiH, not Republika Srpska; is that right? The old MUP.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it clear to you that this was a meeting, really, about how the MUP was divide -- going to divide?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That's not how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, just let's move on and have a look at the conclusions for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No -- sorry, move on. That's the fourth page in English and the fifth page in -- sorry, one, two, three, four -- sixth page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 3: "The Serbian collegium of the SR BH MUP is hereby instructed to carry out all the preparations necessary for the functioning of the Serbian MUP, after the promulgation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution." What, in your view, does that mean, if not, that there is to be a division of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: It means exactly what it says. I did not participate in the drafting of these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the conclusions presumably had to be agreed on by those who were at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I did not take part in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So it's your testimony, is it, Mr. Tutus, that you were not aware at any stage during the course of this meeting in the Hotel Bosna that what was going on was the drawing up of plans for the division of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I did not understand it that way. I did not experience it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then I should ask you: How did you understand this meeting of nothing but Serb members of the MUP, what did you understand was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I don't know if all of the people present were Serbs, but let's take that they were. I understood as a security briefing about the security situation in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that representatives of the Ministry of Interior were informing us of this situation and that we, from the grass roots, were telling them what kind of problems we were encountering on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if -- if this was a -- a security briefing about the security situation in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then why was it being held in a room in the Hotel Bosna, and -- and not in the CSB, or in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: To me, that was a marginal matter. I never gave it any thought until you asked the question: Why Hotel Bosna? The person who convened it there is the only one who knows. It certainly was more pleasant to meet there than somewhere else. I don't think that matters at all. Sorry, it could have been held in Sarajevo. I mean, I don't know the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But if it's a security briefing being given to the MUP, then the obvious place would be Sarajevo, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, it could have been held there, and it could have been held here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And looking at the names of the people, I think most of whom you did know, it's right, isn't it, there isn't a single non-Serb officer there, police officer?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That I don't know. There could have been among them people who were from mixed marriages but did not declare themselves that way. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't want to spend anymore time on that document. Thank you very much. All right. Can we move on then, please, to the events that followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please -- just a moment. Yes, at document number 40, please. No, I'm sorry, I need -- sorry. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. 39. Yeah. P527.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't know how long you are to be with this document. We are two minutes away from the break. I don't know if you want to wait until we return to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a very short document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRONER
utterances.text: -- and I can deal with it straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document that's dated two days after this meeting and is addressed to the CSB Banja Luka, Zupljanin, and various other places. It says: "Following the conclusions reached at the meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February ... please set up and have a meeting with all senior executives of MUP SR BiH in your area and inform me accordingly." And that's signed by Mr. Mandic. You probably didn't see the document before. But did he have a meeting, Mr. Zupljanin, to discuss the conclusions that had been reached at the 11th of February?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I don't remember that. There were meetings and meetings, but whether any meetings were held on that subject, I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's addressed to a rather odd mixture, isn't it? Three CSBs, and three SJBs, and then the SUP for Sarajevo. Can you give any explanation as to why these particular CSBs and SJBs would have been singled out?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In normal circumstances, if the ministry sent out a dispatch like this -- better be careful about calling it a dispatch, but a document like this, would it go to all CSBs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I think, but it doesn't have to be correct. In my view, this dispatch shows that something is wrong in the MUP, that the situation is difficult, precisely what I was saying when we were looking at that transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I want to ask about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we leave that document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- could we just, just to be on the safe side, that we have fully understood the meaning of it, ask the witness two questions; namely, first of all, who would the senior executives of the MUP SR BiH be? Who -- who would Momcilo Mandic have had in mind when he asked this. And, secondly can we just confirm that the SR BiH is the Serbian -- or the Socialist Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Socialist Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So it's the old --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the old --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But could you just confirm that, Mr. Tutus, rather than me giving evidence. There he is referring to the Socialist Republic, is he not, of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who -- and you heard the Judge's question. Who -- who do you understand to be senior executives?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: It's not very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, would that mean SJB chiefs? Would that include you and the others?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: It could include everyone in the MUP, or anyone in the MUP. It's just not very clear to me. Maybe it refers to the seat of the MUP. Maybe it refers to the centres, or the people who are among the addressees. It's really not quite clear to me. But logically it should refer to those to whom it is addressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Would it refer to -- to people who were members of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I keep telling you, I don't really understand this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think that's as far as we can take that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We apologise for the delay. We were discussing procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we move away this document, I have a supplementary question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tutus, could I just clarify one thing of the response that you provided to Ms. Korner just before the break, when she asked you who were the senior executives of the MUP, and you told us that, you know, you really didn't know and that could be literally anyone. The question that I wanted to put to you was, really, could the senior executives be Muslims as well as Croats and Serbs, or would the instruction from Mr. Momcilo Mandic really mean that what he had in mind was that it would be only the senior executives of Serb ethnicity that should be instructed about the meeting that took place two days earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this document, I don't see that it concerns individuals on the basis of their nationality. I can't draw that conclusion on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Nor can I. This is why I asked you. Well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suppose the only conclusion you can draw, though, is that all the addressees, Zupljanin, Bjelosevic, Stojanovic, Savic, Cvijetic, and Stanisic, can't see who was at Bijeljina. Oh, here, I think it's -- it's Predrag Jerasic, isn't it, in Bijeljina. It's quite difficult to read, but ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I agree with everything that you have said, that's all correct. Jerasic is the name. I think that's the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They were all on the face of it, anyhow, Serbs, whether they came from a mixed marriage or not. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't really want to say what their ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move on very quickly then to the next document that I'd like you to look at, which is the document with the 65 ter number 40 [realtime transcript read in error "48"]. Not yet exhibited. And I just want to ask you about one thing on it. The dates been missed off in the English translation for some unknown reason, but we can see it clearly on the -- in the original version, which is the 2nd of March, 1992. And it's addressed, is it not, to the chief of all SJB security stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, in the English to the third page and, in the B/C/S, to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll try and enlarge it's -- because it's only the last -- it's item number 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 11. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I want you to try and look at, so we'll try enlarging it, yeah. This is a dispatch from Zupljanin. If it was -- if it was addressed to all SJB chiefs, that would include you, would it. That's right? "We call your attention once again to the obligation imposed by the instruction on urgent, regular, and interim reports on all incidents of security significance?" Was that -- was Zupljanin concerned that people should report regularly on -- on -- on matters to him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. That's all -- the rest of the documents concern with -- with -- on the security situation, and I don't want to trouble with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in that event, as it's not yet exhibited, may it be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is it on your list of documents for use with this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's tab 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, document number 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Why can't I find it? Oh, you said 40? In the record it is said 48. That's why I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, right. I see. Right. It's 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's why I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P1078 Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, then at the actual split that took place in the MUP. Could you have a look, please, at document number -- sorry, it's already an exhibit, P353. Oh, MFI for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the, I suppose now, famous Mandic telegram of the 31st of March, 1992, addressed to, amongst many addressees, SJB to the chief. And I think when you were asked about this in interview, is this right, you said you remembered receiving this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, if that's what I said, then it's probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I know it's a long time ago now, but this telegram from Momcilo Mandic saying that the Republika Srpska Assembly, or the Serbian People of Assembly, had promulgated the constitution and that Mico Stanisic had been made the minister of the interior, isn't that something that was quite dramatic, in your view?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, it was quite a change. But I wouldn't say that it was dramatic. But, yes, it was a significant change.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Hmm. And were you surprised at all that this had happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I followed the media and the events that preceded this, and on the basis of those events and media coverage, I would say that this was to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So did you get, as the chief the SJB, a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I can't remember, but it's addressed to SJBs so I assume so. But I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it -- it actually changed, didn't it, for example, the -- the number of CSBs, although Banja Luka still remained.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And instead of reporting to Mr. Delimustafic, as minister of the interior in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you -- you would be reporting to Mico Stanisic, wouldn't you, indirectly, obviously, through the CSBs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told it was MFI'd through another witness because they said he wasn't the relevant witness to take it, but as this witness was the chief the SJB and even though he can't remember now whether he got or not, it seems appropriate to admit it through this witness. Otherwise, I will admit it through the next witness but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, I would like you to look now, please, at a document that came from Mr. Delimustafic which unfortunately is not the way it ought to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. I just -- I lost the track what -- what is the -- the -- the P number of this document? If you can just ... Oh, thank you. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, could you look, please, at document 130 -- sorry. 1D136. It's already admitted. On the very same day, after the telegram by Momcilo Mandic had been sent, Mr. Delimustafic sent a document, didn't he, to -- again, addressed to all the chiefs of the SJBs. And do you remember Mr. Delimustafic commenting on Mr. Mandic's telegram, by way of this -- this particular telegram?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I remember that this fax was received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Delimustafic said that this was destructive to the unity of the MUP, and he asks near the end of that first paragraph: "Obviously these -- there are problems in leadership, and I appeal to all ministry workers to stay out of and above them and to continue" -- I think it's "resolving," "very responsible and honourable work and tasks entrusted to them in the existing organisation of the MUP." Did you pass on to those who were your subordinates in any way the fact that Mr. Delimustafic was appealing for unity and that your subordinates had a choice about whether to join the Serbian MUP or remain within the MUP BiH?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: When you see the list of addressees, you can see that it was addressed to the CSB, the SUP in Sarajevo, public security stations, and then it says all police stations. So Minister Delimustafic sent this to the lowest level organisational units at the time, and it was possible for everyone to be familiar with the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So does that mean you didn't actually specifically hold a meeting of your subordinate police stations or subordinates within the SJB to discuss this matter?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: We didn't hold meetings of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you regard this as a major step?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Before this arrived, as far as I know, the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina had adopted a constitution and promulgated a Law on Internal Affairs. If that's the case, and I think it is, then we had to abide by the provisions of that constitution and of those laws. There was a crisis in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a result of which the relationships changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever consider that this decision to set up a separate police force, was likely to -- if not lead to armed conflict, certainly not resile from the -- the concept of an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I didn't believe that it should lead to an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Maybe not in Banja Luka, but what about other areas where there was a much more mixed population of Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. Did you ever think about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: From the very outset, I thought about it, when the former Yugoslavia started breaking up. I could see where things were going, but in my assessment, there shouldn't have been a conflict between reasonable people, but when a state disintegrates you can expect all sort of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, before we look at what happened in Banja Luka at the beginning of April, can we look, please, at one more document, which is document 1 -- well, actually, this is actually dealing with the events of -- yes, beginning of April. Okay, let's start with 1D137, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is, again, addressed -- it's from the CSB Banja Luka, dated the 3rd of April, but it's addressed to the chiefs in -- in the SJBs within the area of the centre, and it's also sent to the Serbian Ministry of Interior amongst other places. And it says: "In line with the dispatch," it begins, "from the SRBH MUP collegium dated the 2nd of April concerning the reorganisation internal affairs organs and their security services that has begun, a professional collegium of security service centres chief was held in Banja Luka, CSB." That was the day before, as we shall see from this document, the SOS set up the barricades. Now, do you remember attending the collegium on the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I didn't attend. I wasn't a member of the collegium of CSBs. I was a member of the professional council.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So that was entirely for -- it wasn't an expanded, as it were, meeting. It was just the --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we go, please, in the English to page 3, and in the B/C/S to the second page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This document, which went out under Zupljanin's name, talks, under 2, of the "erection of the barricades at the approaches to Banja Luka, and then the town itself, by members of the Serbian Defence Forces who presented Banja Luka municipality Crisis Staff with certain conditions, which were accepted after lengthy discussions." And then one of the conditions was that the application of the Law on Internal Affairs begin immediately and that insignia envisaged by this law be introduced and solemn declarations signed. "All these activities must be carried out and concluded by 6 April ..." And then: "The officer will distribute berets and insignia for active police workers at the professional collegium, as well as special a number of forms for solemn declaration which workers will sign the same day before the SJB chief or another person authorised by the SJB chief. I would like to remind you the text of the solemn declaration is identical to that of the solemn declaration in the pervious Law on Internal Affairs." I want to come back to the question of the SOS. But the solemn declaration which we discussed and briefly before when we were looking at the personnel in the SJB, did you yourself have to sign such a declaration?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: According to the law, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I think I did. I most probably did. I can't remember exactly, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This order says that the workers have to sign before you or another person authorised by you. Did your workers in the SJBs and in the police stations which came under your authority, did they sign in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Not in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- I mean, it says here "before the SJB chief." Did you authorise someone else?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I visited the police stations and I was present at a meeting of the crime police in certain organisational units, and I informed them of the task. We called people in accordance with the law, asked them to sign a solemn declaration, and we said we should continue working as we had to date. Those who wanted to sign the document did so. They signed it later in front of their leaders, and those who didn't wanted to sign, well, that was a matter of their goodwill.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But those who didn't want to sign, as we shall see later, there was no question but that they could not stay in their jobs, was there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, in a document, it said that those who didn't sign would be dismissed. Employment would be terminated for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I don't know what the procedure was. It was the department for legal and personnel affairs in the CSB that was responsible for these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But as we saw earlier today, when Mr. Riling didn't sign, he was no longer allowed to work there, was he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, it's not that he couldn't. He left of his own free will. He got up, he left the office. He said -- or he told me, I don't want to work here anymore and he left. Even if I asked him to remain, to continue working with us, even if I said that nothing was going to change, that we weren't going to get involved with politics -- well, there were three or four employee who got up and left. All the others signed the document in front of their superiors. And I think the statements were sent to this department for legal and personnel affairs within the CSB, and it was for that department to deal with these signed documents then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now can we look, please, at the Glas article about the events of the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at a document, P53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, while the document is coming up on the screen, can I ask a question to the witness. Mr. Witness, you said several people for -- I think you said immediately stood up when they were asked to sign. They refused and they left, and they said we don't want to work here anymore. Could you tell me why they reacted this way? What was the problem there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That station commander in Budzak, Mr. Vinko, the policemen knew in advance that this declaration would be up for signing, and then he stood up and said, I'm not going to sign. Those who share my opinion should stand up and walk out with me. Three or four workers did stand up and walked out. One of them approached me and said, Chief, are criminals going to be working together with us in the service? If you can guarantee they won't, we'll stay. And it was about Croats. And I said, As long as I am chief, criminals won't be working with us in the service. So a lot of Croats and Muslims did stay on at this station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You didn't explain to me why this solemn declaration triggered this reaction. That's what I want to know. Why did this solemn declaration made those people leave their jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only tell you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... know your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it's because in Bosnia and Herzegovina the multi-party elections resulted in ethnic rifts and ethnic tensions escalated also in the ranks of people who joined the service and who were sensitive to these ethnic matters and that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the Glas article, virtually additional on what happened in Banja Luka in -- on the 3rd of April. I wanted you to look, please, first of all -- well, first I should ask you, I think you saw this at the time it was published, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can we look in the English, it's on the well, I suppose... sorry. Before we look at specific things. When you were arrived in Banja Luka this morning -- this morning. That morning, were you stopped at the barricades?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who were at the barricades?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you were stopped, what did the men -- first of all, how many -- can you remember how many men were at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: In my estimate, around ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were they armed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did they want when they stopped you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: They asked to see my vehicle registration papers and my driving licence. They wanted to check on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hand them over?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you in civilian clothes or in uniform?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So when you refused to hand over your driving licence -- oh, I'm sorry. I should ask you this. Did you tell them who you were?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you refused to hand over your driving licence and your registration papers, what -- what did they say, or do?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: They were aggressive. One of them trained his rifle at me, and I said, Shoot, if you think that's the solution. Then another one sort of pushed his rifle away and said, Come on, you're going to shoot the chief. One of them obviously recognised me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they let you go after that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes. The one who pushed away the rifle of the other one said, Go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask them who they were and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: They said they were Serbian Defence Forces and they were running checks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- had you ever -- had you heard of the Serbian Defence Forces before this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know what the Serbian Defence Forces were?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And here were a group of armed men setting up barricades in Banja Luka, and you were a police officer. What was -- what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: When I got a report from the operative duty officer around 3.00 a.m. that there were armed group of men taking over the main features in the town, I immediately informed the President of the municipality and told him to go to his work immediately. He asked me to join him and that's how I headed towards the Assembly, joined the President, and told him what was going on. What had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Why wasn't the first thing you did to ring up Stojan Zupljanin and say, There appear to be armed men in the streets setting up barricades. What are we going to do?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: We shared operative duty service within the CSB and it's implied, it goes without saying that he gets reports at the same time when I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I understand that. But you got the report from the operative duty officer that there were these armed mean taking over the main features of town. Why didn't you immediately ring Stojan Zupljanin and say, We need to coordinate our efforts about this, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: When I received that report, it was 3.00 a.m. It went without saying that the operative duty officer had done his job, and it was his job to inform both him and me. That's in his job description.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you informed the President of the municipality. Is that Mr. Radic, Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so when you were stopped, this was around 3.00 a.m. in the morning, was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Maybe half an hour later, the time it took me to get dressed and leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you go and you meet the President of the municipality. And you join -- you go to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you prevented from reaching the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Only the stop at the check-point. That was the only problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where was the check-point that you were stopped at?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: At the bridge by the university, where the students' hostel is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you got to the Assembly building, was Mr. Radic there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, he was already there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who else was there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: He was alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Where was Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So there's you and Mr. Radic and no one else. What do you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, then President Radic invited other people that he thought should be invited. He left the office occasionally meeting other people. Then he convened some sort of meeting, and it was agreed at that meeting that he should negotiate with those people and see what they want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At any stage, was Mr. Zupljanin involved in this, as head of the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of meetings, and he attended these meetings where we discussed how to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At that stage, on the 3rd of April, how many police officers were there in Banja Luka? I think you were asked about this in interview.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I think it's verifiable exactly how many policemen there were. 260 -- 250, I think. I'm not sure, really, about the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But because you were asked about this in your first interview, you went and did a check. And I can show you the page in the interview where you dealt with this, if you like. But did you tell the investigator that: "There were 338 active employees under my command." It's page 6 of the interview of 2004. Does that figure sound correct to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the exact number which includes the employees who were not police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So by active employees, you're including the clerical staff and people like that, are you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you think now it was about 200 -- I'm sorry, just ... 250, 260 actual police officers. All right. And how many -- you had seen about ten men at the barricade that you were stopped at. Roughly how many members of the SOS were there from the information you got?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I didn't stay long at the President's office. Just until he said there would be negotiating. I went to the public security station. I convened my associates, and they informed me that there were around 200 armed men around town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it occur to you -- at that stage telephone Mr. Zupljanin and say that perhaps reinforcements ought to be got? Because he had the power, didn't he, to order the SJBs under his command to provide police officers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: We were there together at the meeting, with President Radic. And on the basis of information we had, I was of the same opinion, that we must look for a political solution, that it can't be solved by use of force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why a political solution when there were armed men in the streets of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Because they were armed, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And in normal circumstances, would you, the police force, allow armed men to set up barricades in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: If the circumstances had been normal, those people would not have had -- not have been armed, and they wouldn't even have had a chance to put up a barricade. But the circumstances were not normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the -- in Banja Luka you had the headquarters, didn't you, of the -- what was then the 6th Krajina Corps of the JNA? The 5th Krajina Corps. Yeah, 5th.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes. But it was before the adoption of the constitution. I don't know exactly when that 5th Krajina Corps grew into the 1st Krajina Corps. In the times of Yugoslavia, it was the 5th Krajina Corps. But I think by the time we are discussing, the 1st Krajina Corps had already been established. But I'm not quite sure about what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry. We know from other evidence that it wasn't established until after the 12th of May. Did anybody suggest that you should go to the army for assistance in getting rid of these armed thugs in the street?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I saw General Talic when he came to see President Radic at that time, and I believe that's what they talked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- so General Talic came to this meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: No. No, he was not at the meeting. But it was during one of those days, a few days before or after, I went to see President Radic. We often had these blitz meetings about the situation around town. Once when I went to see him, I had to wait for his meeting with General Talic to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to understand, and for the purposes of the Trial Chamber as well, why was that, given that this was the worse kind of breach of law and order that could take place, no one suggested doing anything else other than negotiate.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Well, I personally think that the police forces, the security forces were unable at that time to neutralise them. Why they had not been neutralize before, I don't really know, but I know the army was involved in the negotiations, and General Kelecevic was present at one of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you at any stage ever get the feeling or the idea from anything that was said - not the feeling, the idea - that this was a politically organised and staged takeover?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: I would not put it that way. The political scene in Bosnia and Herzegovina was very volatile at the time. There were very ugly dispatches coming from the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Ministry of Interior that could have upset the citizens because they were all published.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let look at, shall we, at the demands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we now look, please, at the demands of the SDS, which I think you should find on page -- I'm not -- actually, I'm not clear. I forgot to mark this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you see Serb -- the headline on the first page, "Serbian Defence Forces Proclamation"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can we in the English -- can we in the English, please, go to the second page, please. It starts: "We Serbian patriot, members of the JNA, reservist, volunteers, citizens of Banja Luka ... organised in the SOS have decided on this step because of a new genocide against Serbian people and the failure of all mechanisms for the protection of the Serbian people." And then it says, under that -- the demands. We can move the page up a little bit.
